claim: The grid-layout of calbindin-positive pyramidal-cells in layer-2 of medial entorhinal cortex emerged around birth in rats.
source: The grid-layout and cholinergic-innervation of calbindin-positive pyramidal-cells in layer-2 emerged around birth while reelin-positive stellate-cells were scattered throughout development.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical data showing calbindin+ patches at P0 with grid-like arrangement (Figure 2a-c).

claim: Cholinergic-innervation of calbindin-positive pyramidal-cells in layer-2 of medial entorhinal cortex emerged around birth in rats.
source: The grid-layout and cholinergic-innervation of calbindin-positive pyramidal-cells in layer-2 emerged around birth while reelin-positive stellate-cells were scattered throughout development.
evidence: Supported by acetylcholinesterase staining showing overlap with calbindin patches at P4 (Figure 2g-i).

claim: Reelin-positive stellate-cells in layer-2 of medial entorhinal cortex were scattered throughout development.
source: The grid-layout and cholinergic-innervation of calbindin-positive pyramidal-cells in layer-2 emerged around birth while reelin-positive stellate-cells were scattered throughout development.
evidence: Supported by reelin immunostaining showing lack of periodicity at P4 and in adults (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: Layer-3 and parasubiculum neurons had a transient calbindin-expression, which declined with age.
source: Layer-3 and parasubiculum neurons had a transient calbindin-expression, which declined with age.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing calbindin+ neuronal density decreased from 955 ± 315 in P4-P8 rats to 141 ± 56 in adults (Figure 3i).

claim: Early postnatally, layer-2 pyramidal but not stellate-cells co-localized with doublecortin.
source: Early postnatally, layer-2 pyramidal but not stellate-cells co-localized with doublecortin – a marker of immature neurons – suggesting delayed functional-maturation of pyramidal-cells.
evidence: Supported by spatial cross-correlations showing higher overlap of doublecortin with calbindin (0.54 ± 0.10) than with reelin (0.08 ± 0.13) (Figure 7e).

claim: Doublecortin is a marker of immature neurons.
source: Early postnatally, layer-2 pyramidal but not stellate-cells co-localized with doublecortin – a marker of immature neurons – suggesting delayed functional-maturation of pyramidal-cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature on doublecortin as a marker for immature neurons (Brown et al., 2003).

claim: The co-localization of doublecortin with layer-2 pyramidal cells suggests delayed functional-maturation of pyramidal-cells.
source: Early postnatally, layer-2 pyramidal but not stellate-cells co-localized with doublecortin – a marker of immature neurons – suggesting delayed functional-maturation of pyramidal-cells.
evidence: Based on inference from doublecortin expression pattern indicating structural immaturity.

claim: Calbindin-expression in layer-3 neurons decreased progressively from dorsal-to-ventral in medial entorhinal cortex.
source: Three observations indicated a dorsal-to-ventral maturation of entorhinal cortex and parasubiculum: (i) calbindin-expression in layer-3 neurons decreased progressively from dorsal-to-ventral, (ii) doublecortin in layer-2 calbindin-positive-patches disappeared dorsally before ventrally, and (iii) wolframin-expression emerged earlier in dorsal than ventral parasubiculum.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing significantly lower densities in dorsal (225 ± 96 cells/mm2) versus ventral (449 ± 161 cells/mm2) MEC in P12-P16 rats (Figure 5d).

claim: Doublecortin in layer-2 calbindin-positive-patches disappeared dorsally before ventrally in medial entorhinal cortex.
source: Three observations indicated a dorsal-to-ventral maturation of entorhinal cortex and parasubiculum: (i) calbindin-expression in layer-3 neurons decreased progressively from dorsal-to-ventral, (ii) doublecortin in layer-2 calbindin-positive-patches disappeared dorsally before ventrally, and (iii) wolframin-expression emerged earlier in dorsal than ventral parasubiculum.
evidence: Supported by spatial cross-correlations showing low correlations in dorsal (0.14 ± 0.17) but high overlap in ventral (0.60 ± 0.07) regions in P16-P20 rats (Figure 6m).

claim: Wolframin-expression emerged earlier in dorsal than ventral parasubiculum.
source: Three observations indicated a dorsal-to-ventral maturation of entorhinal cortex and parasubiculum: (i) calbindin-expression in layer-3 neurons decreased progressively from dorsal-to-ventral, (ii) doublecortin in layer-2 calbindin-positive-patches disappeared dorsally before ventrally, and (iii) wolframin-expression emerged earlier in dorsal than ventral parasubiculum.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining showing wolframin present in dorsal ~10% of PaS at P4, ~40% at P8, and 100% at P20 (Figure 8).

claim: The early appearance of calbindin-pyramidal-grid-organization in layer-2 suggests that this pattern is instructed by genetic information rather than experience.
source: The early appearance of calbindin-pyramidal-grid-organization in layer-2 suggests that this pattern is instructed by genetic information rather than experience.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that grid-like arrangement is present at birth (P0), before spatial experience.

claim: Superficial-layer-microcircuits mature earlier in dorsal entorhinal cortex, where small spatial-scales are represented.
source: Superficial-layer-microcircuits mature earlier in dorsal entorhinal cortex, where small spatial-scales are represented.
evidence: Based on inference from dorsal-to-ventral maturation gradient and established knowledge that dorsal MEC represents smaller spatial scales (Hafting et al., 2005; Stensola et al., 2012).

claim: Maturation of ventral-entorhinal-microcircuits – representing larger spatial-scales – follows later around the onset of exploratory behavior.
source: Maturation of ventral-entorhinal-microcircuits – representing larger spatial-scales – follows later around the onset of exploratory behavior.
evidence: Based on inference from temporal correlation between ventral MEC maturation and onset of exploratory behavior around end of second postnatal week (Wills et al., 2014; Bulut and Altman, 1974).

claim: Layer 2 of MEC contains two types of principal cells, stellate and pyramidal cells in adult animals.
source: In adult animals, layer 2 of MEC contains two types of principal cells, stellate and pyramidal cells (Alonso and Klink, 1993; Germroth et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Stellate and pyramidal neurons are distinct in their intrinsic conductance.
source: Stellate and pyramidal neurons are distinct in their intrinsic conductance (Alonso and Llinás, 1989; Klink and Alonso, 1997), immunoreactivity (Varga et al., 2010), projections (Lingenhöhl and Finch, 1991; Canto and Witter, 2012) and inhibitory inputs (Varga et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Stellate and pyramidal neurons are distinct in their immunoreactivity.
source: Stellate and pyramidal neurons are distinct in their intrinsic conductance (Alonso and Llinás, 1989; Klink and Alonso, 1997), immunoreactivity (Varga et al., 2010), projections (Lingenhöhl and Finch, 1991; Canto and Witter, 2012) and inhibitory inputs (Varga et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Stellate and pyramidal neurons are distinct in their projections.
source: Stellate and pyramidal neurons are distinct in their intrinsic conductance (Alonso and Llinás, 1989; Klink and Alonso, 1997), immunoreactivity (Varga et al., 2010), projections (Lingenhöhl and Finch, 1991; Canto and Witter, 2012) and inhibitory inputs (Varga et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Stellate and pyramidal neurons are distinct in their inhibitory inputs.
source: Stellate and pyramidal neurons are distinct in their intrinsic conductance (Alonso and Llinás, 1989; Klink and Alonso, 1997), immunoreactivity (Varga et al., 2010), projections (Lingenhöhl and Finch, 1991; Canto and Witter, 2012) and inhibitory inputs (Varga et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pyramidal neurons in layer 2 of MEC can be identified by calbindin-immuno-reactivity.
source: Pyramidal neurons in layer 2 of MEC can be identified by calbindin-immuno-reactivity (Varga et al., 2010) and are clustered in patches across various mammalian species (Fujimaru and Kosaka, 1996; Ray et al., 2014; Naumann et al., 2016), while stellate cells can be identified by reelin-immuno-reactivity (Varga et al., 2010) and a lack of structural periodicity (Ray et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pyramidal neurons in layer 2 of MEC are clustered in patches across various mammalian species.
source: Pyramidal neurons in layer 2 of MEC can be identified by calbindin-immuno-reactivity (Varga et al., 2010) and are clustered in patches across various mammalian species (Fujimaru and Kosaka, 1996; Ray et al., 2014; Naumann et al., 2016), while stellate cells can be identified by reelin-immuno-reactivity (Varga et al., 2010) and a lack of structural periodicity (Ray et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Stellate cells in layer 2 of MEC can be identified by reelin-immuno-reactivity.
source: Pyramidal neurons in layer 2 of MEC can be identified by calbindin-immuno-reactivity (Varga et al., 2010) and are clustered in patches across various mammalian species (Fujimaru and Kosaka, 1996; Ray et al., 2014; Naumann et al., 2016), while stellate cells can be identified by reelin-immuno-reactivity (Varga et al., 2010) and a lack of structural periodicity (Ray et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Stellate cells in layer 2 of MEC exhibit a lack of structural periodicity.
source: Pyramidal neurons in layer 2 of MEC can be identified by calbindin-immuno-reactivity (Varga et al., 2010) and are clustered in patches across various mammalian species (Fujimaru and Kosaka, 1996; Ray et al., 2014; Naumann et al., 2016), while stellate cells can be identified by reelin-immuno-reactivity (Varga et al., 2010) and a lack of structural periodicity (Ray et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In rodents, the grid-like arrangement of pyramidal cell patches is aligned to cholinergic inputs.
source: In rodents, the grid-like arrangement of pyramidal cell patches is aligned to cholinergic inputs (Ray et al., 2014; Naumann et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: About a third of all cells in layer 2 of MEC exhibit spatial tuning with grid, border, irregular and head-directional discharges being present.
source: Functionally, about a third of all cells in layer 2 exhibit spatial tuning with grid, border, irregular and head-directional discharges being present (Tang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Neurons in layer 3 of MEC are characterized by rather homogenous in vitro intrinsic and in vivo spatiotemporal properties.
source: Neurons in layer 3 of MEC are characterized by rather homogenous in vitro intrinsic and in vivo spatiotemporal properties (Tang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A majority of cells in layer 3 of MEC exhibit a lack of spatial modulation.
source: A majority of cells exhibit a lack of spatial modulation, and the remaining are mainly dominated by irregular spatial responses (Tang et al., 2015) with a fraction also exhibiting grid, border and head-directional responses (Boccara et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The remaining spatially modulated cells in layer 3 of MEC are mainly dominated by irregular spatial responses.
source: A majority of cells exhibit a lack of spatial modulation, and the remaining are mainly dominated by irregular spatial responses (Tang et al., 2015) with a fraction also exhibiting grid, border and head-directional responses (Boccara et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A fraction of cells in layer 3 of MEC exhibit grid, border and head-directional responses.
source: A majority of cells exhibit a lack of spatial modulation, and the remaining are mainly dominated by irregular spatial responses (Tang et al., 2015) with a fraction also exhibiting grid, border and head-directional responses (Boccara et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The parasubiculum is a long and narrow structure flanking the dorsal and medial extremities of MEC.
source: The parasubiculum is a long and narrow structure flanking the dorsal and medial extremities of MEC (Video 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Video 1 showing anatomical location.

claim: The superficial parasubiculum, corresponding to layer 1 of MEC is divided into large clusters.
source: The superficial parasubiculum, corresponding to layer 1 of MEC is divided into large clusters, while the deeper part, corresponding to layers 2 and 3 of MEC, is rather homogenous (Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The deeper part of parasubiculum, corresponding to layers 2 and 3 of MEC, is rather homogenous.
source: The superficial parasubiculum, corresponding to layer 1 of MEC is divided into large clusters, while the deeper part, corresponding to layers 2 and 3 of MEC, is rather homogenous (Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A majority of the cells of PaS show spatially tuned responses, and include grid, border, head-directional and irregular spatial cells.
source: In terms of functional tuning of cells, a majority of the cells of PaS show spatially tuned responses, and include grid, border, head-directional and irregular spatial cells (Boccara et al., 2010; Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The majority of brain development in rats takes place within the first few weeks postnatally.
source: The majority of the brain development takes place within the first few weeks postnatally (Figure 1a), with the brain size increasing 1000% from 0.12 ± 0.00 g at E18 (mean ± SD; n=3) to 1.23 ± 0.07 g at P12 (n=5).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of brain weight showing 1000% increase from E18 to P12.

claim: Rat brain size increases 1000% from 0.12 ± 0.00 g at E18 to 1.23 ± 0.07 g at P12.
source: The majority of the brain development takes place within the first few weeks postnatally (Figure 1a), with the brain size increasing 1000% from 0.12 ± 0.00 g at E18 (mean ± SD; n=3) to 1.23 ± 0.07 g at P12 (n=5).
evidence: Supported by direct measurements of brain weight.

claim: After P12, rat brain growth plateaus to ~25% with the brain weighing 1.71 ± 0.08 g at P24 and 2.11 ± 0.14 g in adults.
source: Subsequently, the growth plateaus to ~25% with the brain weighing 1.71 ± 0.08 g at P24 (n=6) and having a weight of 2.11 ± 0.14 g in adults (n=9) (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by direct measurements of brain weight.

claim: The superficial layers (layers 1–3) of the MEC double in thickness during the first postnatal week from 243 ± 35 μm at P0 to 652 ± 50 μm at P12.
source: The superficial layers (layers 1–3) of the MEC (Figure 1c) double in thickness during this early postnatal period from 243 ± 35 μm at P0 (mean ± SD; n=21, 4 rats) to 652 ± 50 μm at P12 (n=24, 4 rats).
evidence: Supported by direct measurements of layer thickness.

claim: The deeper layers (layers 4–6) of MEC increase in thickness from 167 ± 21 μm at P0 to 329 ± 54 μm at P12.
source: A similar increase is also observed in the deeper layers (layers 4–6) from 167 ± 21 μm at P0 (n=21, 4 rats) to 329 ± 54 μm at P12 (n=24, 4 rats).
evidence: Supported by direct measurements of layer thickness.

claim: The overall thickness of MEC plateaus around P12 to 981 ± 81 μm and remains at 882 ± 78 μm in adults.
source: The overall thickness plateaus around this point to 981 ± 81 μm at P12 (n=24, 4 rats) and remains at 882 ± 78 μm in adults (n=24, 4 rats) (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by direct measurements of total MEC thickness.

claim: Layer 2 accounts for ~20% of MEC thickness during development.
source: Proportionally, the thickness of the layers remains similar during development, with layer 2 accounting for ~20% and layers 3 and 5/6 each accounting for ~30% of the MEC.
evidence: Supported by proportional analysis of layer thickness measurements.

claim: Layers 3 and 5/6 each account for ~30% of MEC thickness during development.
source: Proportionally, the thickness of the layers remains similar during development, with layer 2 accounting for ~20% and layers 3 and 5/6 each accounting for ~30% of the MEC.
evidence: Supported by proportional analysis of layer thickness measurements.

claim: Layers 1 and 4 are the thinnest at about 10% and 5% of the total MEC thickness respectively.
source: Layers 1 and 4 are the thinnest at about 10% and 5% of the total thickness respectively (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by proportional analysis of layer thickness measurements.

claim: Calbindin+ neurons in the MEC exhibited clustering, forming patches at P0.
source: From the earliest postnatal stages, calbindin+ neurons in the MEC exhibited clustering, forming patches at P0 (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical staining showing calbindin+ patches at P0.

claim: The calbindin+ patches at P0 exhibited a grid-like regular arrangement, similar to that observed in adults.
source: The calbindin+ patches at P0 exhibited a grid-like (Figure 2a,b) regular arrangement (Figure 2c), determined by spatial autocorrelation analysis and grid scores, similar to that observed in adults (Ray et al., 2014; Naumann et al., 2016, Figure 2d–f).
evidence: Supported by spatial autocorrelation analysis showing grid score of 0.59 at P0 and comparison to adult data.

claim: Stellate cells were present in early postnatal stages and exhibited a lack of periodicity.
source: Similar preparations for visualizing stellate cells by reelin-immunoreactivity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), exhibited the presence of stellate cells in early postnatal stages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,b) and a lack of periodicity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c), similar to observations made in adults (Ray et al., 2014, Figure 2—figure supplement 1d–f).
evidence: Supported by reelin immunostaining and spatial autocorrelation analysis showing grid score of -0.09 at P4.

claim: Calbindin+ pyramidal neurons in the MEC received preferential cholinergic innervation early postnatally.
source: Calbindin+ pyramidal neurons in the MEC (Figure 2g) also received preferential cholinergic innervation early postnatally (Figure 2h–i), similar to adults (Ray et al., 2014; Naumann et al., 2016, Figure 2j–l).
evidence: Supported by acetylcholinesterase staining showing overlap with calbindin patches at P4.

claim: In the parasubiculum, a transient presence of calbindin was observed with ~15 clusters of calbindin+ neurons at P0 and P4.
source: In the parasubiculum, a transient presence of calbindin was observed with ~15 clusters of calbindin+ neurons at P0 (Figure 2a) and P4 (Figure 2g).
evidence: Supported by calbindin immunostaining showing clusters in parasubiculum at P0 and P4.

claim: Calbindin expression in parasubiculum was curtailed in older animals, with only a calbindin+ stripe persisting in adults.
source: This expression was curtailed in older animals, with only a calbindin+ stripe persisting in adults (Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by calbindin immunostaining showing reduced expression in adult parasubiculum.

claim: Indications of calbindin+ neuronal clusters were visible prenatally at E18.
source: Indications of calbindin+ neuronal clusters were visible prenatally at E18 (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by calbindin immunostaining at E18.

claim: The calbindin+ patches in the MEC did not exhibit clustering of their dendrites at E18 and P0.
source: However, the calbindin+ patches in the MEC did not exhibit clustering of their dendrites, as previously described in adults (Ray et al., 2014) at E18 and P0 (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: Supported by visual inspection of calbindin immunostaining showing lack of dendritic clustering at E18 and P0.

claim: Some dendritic clustering of calbindin+ pyramidal neurons could be observed at P4.
source: Some dendritic clustering could be observed at P4 (Figure 3c), while from P8 (Figure 3d–h) the dendritic clustering of calbindin+ pyramidal neurons was similar to that in adults.
evidence: Supported by visual inspection of calbindin immunostaining at P4.

claim: From P8, the dendritic clustering of calbindin+ pyramidal neurons was similar to that in adults.
source: Some dendritic clustering could be observed at P4 (Figure 3c), while from P8 (Figure 3d–h) the dendritic clustering of calbindin+ pyramidal neurons was similar to that in adults.
evidence: Supported by visual inspection of calbindin immunostaining from P8 onwards.

claim: The number of calbindin+ neurons in layer 3 declined progressively from prenatal stages to P20.
source: In layer 3 of the MEC, we observed a transient presence of calbindin expression. The number of calbindin+ neurons in layer 3 declined progressively from prenatal stages to P20 (Figure 3a–g), where it attained adult-like levels with rarely any calbindin+ neurons in layer 3 (Figure 3h).
evidence: Supported by visual inspection and quantification of calbindin+ neurons in layer 3 across developmental stages.

claim: Calbindin+ neuronal density in layer 3 decreased from 955 ± 315 in P4-P8 rats to 333 ± 99 in P12-P16 rats to 141 ± 56 in adults.
source: Quantitatively, calbindin+ neuronal density (calbindin+ neurons per mm2) decreased from 955 ± 315 (mean ± SD; count refers to n=3776 neurons in 8 rats) in P4-P8 rats to 333 ± 99 (n=2104 neurons, 8 rats) in P12-P16 rats to 141 ± 56 (n=828 neurons, 7 rats) in adults (Figure 3i).
evidence: Supported by quantitative cell counts of calbindin+ neurons in layer 3.

claim: Reelin was present in layer 2 from early postnatal stages.
source: Reelin was present in layer 2 from early postnatal stages (Figure 4a; Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,b), though the most prominent reelin-immunoreactive cells in the first two postnatal weeks were present in layer 1 (Figure 4a–c).
evidence: Supported by reelin immunostaining showing presence in layer 2 at early postnatal stages.

claim: The most prominent reelin-immunoreactive cells in the first two postnatal weeks were present in layer 1.
source: Reelin was present in layer 2 from early postnatal stages (Figure 4a; Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,b), though the most prominent reelin-immunoreactive cells in the first two postnatal weeks were present in layer 1 (Figure 4a–c).
evidence: Supported by reelin immunostaining showing strongest expression in layer 1 during first two postnatal weeks.

claim: Reelin expression increased in layer 3 of the MEC from early postnatal stages to P20.
source: Reelin expression increased in layer 3 of the MEC from early postnatal stages to P20 (Figure 4a–e), where it attained adult-like levels (Figure 4f).
evidence: Supported by visual inspection of reelin immunostaining across developmental stages.

claim: Reelin+ neuronal density in layer 3 increased from 729 ± 435 in P4-P8 rats to 1549 ± 115 in P12-P16 rats to 1996 ± 208 in adults.
source: Quantitatively, reelin+ neuronal density in layer 3 increased from 729 ± 435 (n=1405 neurons, 4 rats) in P4-P8 rats to 1549 ± 115 (n=3309 neurons, 3 rats) in P12-P16 rats to 1996 ± 208 (n=5039 neurons, 3 rats) in adults.
evidence: Supported by quantitative cell counts of reelin+ neurons in layer 3.

claim: Most of layer 3 had calbindin+ neurons at P8.
source: Thus, most of layer 3 had calbindin+ neurons at P8 (Figure 5a), only the ventral half of layer 3 showed calbindin expression at P16 (Figure 5b), and in adults calbindin expression was largely absent from layer 3 of MEC (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by calbindin immunostaining showing widespread expression in layer 3 at P8.

claim: Only the ventral half of layer 3 showed calbindin expression at P16.
source: Thus, most of layer 3 had calbindin+ neurons at P8 (Figure 5a), only the ventral half of layer 3 showed calbindin expression at P16 (Figure 5b), and in adults calbindin expression was largely absent from layer 3 of MEC (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by calbindin immunostaining showing restricted expression to ventral half at P16.

claim: In adults, calbindin expression was largely absent from layer 3 of MEC.
source: Thus, most of layer 3 had calbindin+ neurons at P8 (Figure 5a), only the ventral half of layer 3 showed calbindin expression at P16 (Figure 5b), and in adults calbindin expression was largely absent from layer 3 of MEC (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by calbindin immunostaining showing minimal expression in layer 3 in adults.

claim: In P4-P8 rats, equitable densities of calbindin+ cells were observed in dorsal, intermediate and ventral levels of MEC layer 3.
source: Early postnatally, in P4-P8 rats, we observed equitable densities of calbindin+ cells in dorsal, intermediate and ventral levels of MEC (n=3776 neurons, 8 rats).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of calbindin+ cell distribution in layer 3.

claim: In P12-P16 rats, significantly lower densities of calbindin+ cells were observed in the dorsal (225 ± 96 cells/mm2) as opposed to the ventral (449 ± 161 cells/mm2) MEC layer 3.
source: In contrast, around the end of the second postnatal week, in P12-P16 rats, we observed significantly lower densities (p=0.010, Mann-Whitney two tailed) in the dorsal (225 ± 96 cells / mm2), as opposed to the ventral (449 ± 161 cells / mm2) MEC (n=2104 neurons, 8 rats).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis with statistical testing showing significant difference.

claim: In adults, calbindin+ neurons were largely absent in layer 3, but among the remaining population the density waxed from dorsal to intermediate and ventral MEC.
source: In adults (n=828 neurons, 7 rats), calbindin+ neurons were largely absent in layer 3, but among the remaining population the density waxed from dorsal to intermediate and ventral MEC.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of calbindin+ cell distribution in adult layer 3.

claim: The development of reelin expression in layer 3 neurons occurred in equitable proportions in dorsal, intermediate and ventral levels of MEC with increasing age.
source: The development of reelin expression in layer 3 neurons on the other hand (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a–c) occurred in equitable proportions in dorsal, intermediate and ventral levels of MEC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1d) with increasing age.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of reelin+ cell distribution in layer 3 across dorsoventral axis.

claim: Layer 2 calbindin+ patches co-localized with doublecortin throughout layer 2 at P8.
source: The calbindin+ patches (Figure 6a) co-localized with doublecortin (Figure 6b), a well-established marker for immature neurons (Brown et al., 2003) throughout layer 2 at P8 (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: Supported by double immunostaining showing overlap of calbindin and doublecortin at P8.

claim: At P16, the dorsal calbindin+ patches did not express doublecortin, while ventral calbindin+ patches still co-localized with doublecortin.
source: At P16, the dorsal calbindin+ patches (Figure 6e,g) did not express doublecortin (Figure 6f,g), while ventral calbindin+ patches still co-localized with doublecortin (Figure 6h).
evidence: Supported by double immunostaining showing differential doublecortin expression in dorsal versus ventral regions at P16.

claim: In adults, calbindin+ patches did not exhibit doublecortin in either dorsal or ventral parts.
source: In adults, calbindin+ patches (Figure 6i) did not exhibit doublecortin (Figure 6j) in either dorsal (Figure 6k) or ventral (Figure 6l) parts.
evidence: Supported by double immunostaining showing absence of doublecortin in adult calbindin+ patches.

claim: Doublecortin was present throughout the PaS in P8 rats.
source: A similar dorsal-to-ventral development gradient was evident in the PaS, with doublecortin being present throughout the PaS in P8 (Figure 6b), only in the ventral part in P16 (Figure 6f) and not present in adults (Figure 6j).
evidence: Supported by doublecortin immunostaining showing expression throughout PaS at P8.

claim: Doublecortin was present only in the ventral part of PaS in P16 rats.
source: A similar dorsal-to-ventral development gradient was evident in the PaS, with doublecortin being present throughout the PaS in P8 (Figure 6b), only in the ventral part in P16 (Figure 6f) and not present in adults (Figure 6j).
evidence: Supported by doublecortin immunostaining showing restricted expression to ventral PaS at P16.

claim: Doublecortin was not present in PaS in adult rats.
source: A similar dorsal-to-ventral development gradient was evident in the PaS, with doublecortin being present throughout the PaS in P8 (Figure 6b), only in the ventral part in P16 (Figure 6f) and not present in adults (Figure 6j).
evidence: Supported by doublecortin immunostaining showing absence in adult PaS.

claim: P8-P12 rats exhibited a high degree of overlap between calbindin and doublecortin in both dorsal (0.74 ± 0.05) and ventral (0.61 ± 0.10) parts.
source: P8-P12 rats exhibited a high degree of overlap between calbindin and doublecortin in both dorsal (0.74 ± 0.05; mean ± SD, Pearson's cross-correlation coefficient) and ventral (0.61 ± 0.10) parts (n=9 regions, 5 rats).
evidence: Supported by spatial cross-correlation analysis quantifying overlap.

claim: In P16-P20 rats, the dorsal regions showed low correlations (0.14 ± 0.17) between calbindin and doublecortin, while the ventral regions still showed significantly higher overlap (0.60 ± 0.07).
source: In P16-P20 rats (n=16 regions, 8 rats), the dorsal regions showed low correlations (0.14 ± 0.17), while the ventral regions still showed significantly higher overlap (0.60 ± 0.07; p=0.0008, Mann-Whitney two tailed).
evidence: Supported by spatial cross-correlation analysis with statistical testing showing significant difference.

claim: In adults, both dorsal (0.19 ± 0.07) and ventral (0.20 ± 0.07) regions had low overlap between calbindin and doublecortin.
source: In adults (n=7 regions, 4 rats), both dorsal (0.19 ± 0.07) and ventral (0.20 ± 0.07) regions had low overlap.
evidence: Supported by spatial cross-correlation analysis quantifying overlap in adults.

claim: The difference in the Pearson's cross correlation coefficient between overlapping regions and non-overlapping regions was significant at p=0.000001.
source: The difference in the Pearson's cross correlation coefficient between overlapping regions (dorsal and ventral in P8-P12; ventral in P16-P20) and non-overlapping regions (dorsal in P16-P20; dorsal and ventral in adults) was significant at p=0.000001 (Mann-Whitney two tailed).
evidence: Supported by statistical testing of cross-correlation data.

claim: Doublecortin is mostly co-localized with calbindin+ rather than reelin+ neurons in layer 2 of MEC.
source: A closer analysis of the co-localization of the immature neuronal marker doublecortin with calbindin+ pyramidal cells and reelin+ stellate cells (Figure 7a–c) revealed doublecortin to be mostly co-localized with calbindin+ rather than reelin+ neurons (Figure 7d).
evidence: Supported by triple immunostaining showing preferential co-localization with calbindin.

claim: Spatial cross-correlations revealed a greater overlap of doublecortin with calbindin (0.54 ± 0.10) than with reelin (0.08 ± 0.13).
source: Spatial cross-correlations between doublecortin and either calbindin or reelin (Figure 7e; n=8 rats from ages P8 - P20) from triple-immunostained calbindin, reelin and doublecortin regions of layer 2 of the MEC revealed a greater overlap of doublecortin with calbindin (0.54 ± 0.10) than with reelin (0.08 ± 0.13).
evidence: Supported by spatial cross-correlation analysis of triple-stained sections.

claim: The difference in the Pearson's cross correlation coefficient between doublecortin-calbindin and doublecortin-reelin was significant at p=0.0009.
source: This difference in the Pearson's cross correlation coefficient was significant at p=0.0009 (Mann-Whitney two tailed).
evidence: Supported by statistical testing of cross-correlation data.

claim: Wolframin expression starts to appear in the dorsal MEC and the dorsal PaS shortly after birth.
source: Specifically, wolframin expression starts to appear in the dorsal MEC and the dorsal PaS shortly after birth (Figure 8a) and is present only in the dorsal ~10% of the PaS.
evidence: Supported by wolframin immunostaining showing initial expression in dorsal regions at P4.

claim: Wolframin expression is present only in the dorsal ~10% of the PaS at P4.
source: Specifically, wolframin expression starts to appear in the dorsal MEC and the dorsal PaS shortly after birth (Figure 8a) and is present only in the dorsal ~10% of the PaS.
evidence: Supported by wolframin immunostaining showing limited dorsal expression at P4.

claim: Wolframin expression extends progressively more ventrally and covers ~40% of PaS at P8 and ~75% at P12.
source: It extends progressively more ventrally (Figure 8b) and covers ~40% at P8 and ~75% at P12 of PaS.
evidence: Supported by wolframin immunostaining showing progressive ventral expansion.

claim: At P20, wolframin is expressed throughout the full extent of medial entorhinal cortex and the parasubiculum.
source: At P20 it is expressed throughout the full extent of medial entorhinal cortex and the parasubiculum (Figure 8c).
evidence: Supported by wolframin immunostaining showing complete coverage at P20.

claim: Neurogenesis in the medial entorhinal cortex is completed prior to E18.
source: Neurogenesis in the medial entorhinal cortex is completed prior to E18 (Bayer, 1980a; 1980b), and at this time the basic laminar organization of medial entorhinal cortex is already evident.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: At E18, the basic laminar organization of medial entorhinal cortex is already evident.
source: Neurogenesis in the medial entorhinal cortex is completed prior to E18 (Bayer, 1980a; 1980b), and at this time the basic laminar organization of medial entorhinal cortex is already evident.
evidence: Supported by observation of laminar structure at E18 and citation to previous literature.

claim: The periodic structure of calbindin+ patches is a result of genetic signaling rather than spatial experience.
source: This observation indicates that the periodic structure of patches is a result of genetic signaling rather than spatial experience.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that periodic structure is present at birth before spatial experience.

claim: Periodic patterns are ubiquitous in nature, and several chemical patterning systems have been explained on the basis of interaction between dynamical systems.
source: Periodic patterns are ubiquitous in nature, and several chemical patterning systems have been explained on the basis of interaction between dynamical systems (Turing, 1952).
evidence: Supported by citation to Turing's work on pattern formation.

claim: It has been suggested that the grid layout of calbindin+ neurons is functionally relevant for grid cell activity.
source: Since it has been suggested that the grid layout of calbindin+ neurons is functionally relevant for grid cell activity (Brecht, 2014), it would be interesting to investigate, whether genetic manipulations would result in changes of layout periodicity and have functional effects.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous speculation.

claim: The dendritic clustering of calbindin+ pyramidal neurons is similar to dendritic development in the neocortex and is established by the end of the first postnatal week.
source: The dendritic clustering of calbindin+ pyramidal neurons is similar to dendritic development in the neocortex (Petit et al., 1988) and is established by the end of the first postnatal week.
evidence: Supported by observation of dendritic clustering from P8 onwards and citation to neocortical development.

claim: The cholinergic innervation of the calbindin+ patches was present by P4 in line with other long-range connectivity patterns in the MEC, which are also established early in development.
source: The cholinergic innervation of the calbindin+ patches was present by P4 in line with other long-range connectivity patterns in the MEC (O'Reilly et al., 2015), which are also established early in development.
evidence: Supported by observation of cholinergic innervation at P4 and citation to previous work on connectivity development.

claim: Reelin is an important protein in cortical layer development.
source: Reelin is an important protein in cortical layer development (D'Arcangelo et al., 1995) and in the early stages of postnatal development we see the strongest reelin expression in layer 1, where reelin secreting Cajal-Retzius cells are involved in radial neuronal migration (Pesold et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on reelin function.

claim: In the early stages of postnatal development, the strongest reelin expression is in layer 1, where reelin secreting Cajal-Retzius cells are involved in radial neuronal migration.
source: Reelin is an important protein in cortical layer development (D'Arcangelo et al., 1995) and in the early stages of postnatal development we see the strongest reelin expression in layer 1, where reelin secreting Cajal-Retzius cells are involved in radial neuronal migration (Pesold et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by observation of reelin expression in layer 1 and citation to previous literature on Cajal-Retzius cells.

claim: Part of the calbindin+ neuronal density decline in layer 3 can be attributed to the increasing brain size.
source: While the density of reelin+ neurons increases, there is a concurrent decline in calbindin+ neuronal density in layer 3 of MEC, though part of the calbindin+ neuronal density decline can be attributed to the increasing brain size.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that brain size increases during the same period.

claim: Transient expression of calbindin has been observed in early postnatal development in the neocortex and midbrain regions.
source: Transient expression of calbindin has been observed in early postnatal development in the neocortex (Hogan and Berman, 1993) and midbrain regions (Liu and Graybiel, 1992), but its functional significance remains largely unknown.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The functional significance of transient calbindin expression remains largely unknown.
source: Transient expression of calbindin has been observed in early postnatal development in the neocortex (Hogan and Berman, 1993) and midbrain regions (Liu and Graybiel, 1992), but its functional significance remains largely unknown.
evidence: Represents a knowledge gap acknowledged in the literature.

claim: At early developmental stages, the parasubiculum and medial entorhinal cortex share a similar organization in calbindin+ patches.
source: Our data show, however, that at early developmental stages the parasubiculum and medial entorhinal cortex share a similar organization in calbindin+ patches.
evidence: Supported by observation of calbindin+ patches in both structures at P0 and P4.

claim: The expression of wolframin in the parasubiculum persists in adults.
source: Additionally, the expression of wolframin in the parasubiculum persists in adults, while calbindin+ neurons in MEC layer 2 also exhibit wolframin (Kitamura et al., 2014) from the end of the first postnatal week.
evidence: Supported by observation of wolframin expression in adult PaS and citation to previous work.

claim: Calbindin+ neurons in MEC layer 2 exhibit wolframin from the end of the first postnatal week.
source: Additionally, the expression of wolframin in the parasubiculum persists in adults, while calbindin+ neurons in MEC layer 2 also exhibit wolframin (Kitamura et al., 2014) from the end of the first postnatal week.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Calbindin is a calcium buffer, and reduces the concentration of intracellular calcium.
source: For instance, calbindin is a calcium buffer, and reduces the concentration of intracellular calcium (Mattson et al., 1991), while wolframin is implicated in increasing intracellular calcium levels (Osman et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on protein function.

claim: Wolframin is implicated in increasing intracellular calcium levels.
source: For instance, calbindin is a calcium buffer, and reduces the concentration of intracellular calcium (Mattson et al., 1991), while wolframin is implicated in increasing intracellular calcium levels (Osman et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature on protein function.

claim: The medial entorhinal cortex and parasubiculum have many similarities in their spatial discharge properties.
source: With the medial entorhinal cortex and parasubiculum having many similarities in their spatial discharge properties (Tang et al., 2014; Boccara et al., 2010; Tang et al., 2016), a structure-function comparison of the wolframin+/transiently-calbindin+ neurons in the parasubiculum and the wolframin+/ permanently-calbindin+ neurons in the medial entorhinal cortex would be worthwhile.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on functional properties.

claim: Homing behavior in rats, as well as spontaneous exploratory behavior develops around the end of second postnatal week.
source: Homing behavior in rats, as well as spontaneous exploratory behavior develops around the end of second postnatal week (Wills et al., 2014; Bulut and Altman, 1974) while spontaneous exploration of larger environments outside the nest emerge towards the end of the third postnatal week (Wills et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on behavioral development.

claim: Spontaneous exploration of larger environments outside the nest emerge towards the end of the third postnatal week.
source: Homing behavior in rats, as well as spontaneous exploratory behavior develops around the end of second postnatal week (Wills et al., 2014; Bulut and Altman, 1974) while spontaneous exploration of larger environments outside the nest emerge towards the end of the third postnatal week (Wills et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature on behavioral development.

claim: The timeline of maturation of calbindin+ patches in the dorsal and ventral MEC is coincident with the development of homing behavior and spontaneous exploration.
source: This is coincident with the timeline of maturation of calbindin+ patches in the dorsal and ventral MEC respectively.
evidence: Based on inference from temporal correlation between structural and behavioral development.

claim: The dorsal MEC represents smaller spatial scales and the ventral MEC progressively larger scales.
source: Since the dorsal MEC represents smaller spatial scales and the ventral MEC progressively larger scales (Hafting et al., 2005; Stensola et al., 2012), these data may indicate that the rat's navigational system matures from small to large scales.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on spatial scale representation.

claim: The rat's navigational system may mature from small to large scales.
source: Since the dorsal MEC represents smaller spatial scales and the ventral MEC progressively larger scales (Hafting et al., 2005; Stensola et al., 2012), these data may indicate that the rat's navigational system matures from small to large scales.
evidence: Based on inference from dorsal-to-ventral maturation gradient and spatial scale representation.

claim: Early eyelid opening experiments have indicated an accelerated development of spatial exploratory behaviour.
source: Early eyelid opening experiments have indicated an accelerated development of spatial exploratory behaviour (Kenny and Turkewitz, 1986; Foreman and Altaha, 1991), and similar experiments might provide insights into whether early behavioral development is accompanied by an accelerated development of the microcircuit underlying spatial navigation.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on experimental manipulations.

claim: The higher co-localization of doublecortin with calbindin+ pyramidal cells than reelin+ stellate cells supports the dichotomy of structure-function relationships exhibited by these two cell types.
source: The higher co-localization of doublecortin with calbindin+ pyramidal cells than reelin+ stellate cells, supports further the dichotomy of structure-function relationships exhibited by these two cell types (Ray et al., 2014; Tang et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on inference from differential doublecortin expression and citation to previous work on cell type differences.

claim: Grid and border cells have been implicated to be largely specific to pyramidal and stellate cells respectively.
source: Grid and border cells have been implicated to be largely specific to pyramidal and stellate cells respectively (Tang et al., 2014)and the delayed structural maturation of pyramidal cells might reflect the delayed functional maturation of grid cells (Wills et al., 2010; Langston et al., 2010), with the converse being applicable to stellate and border cells (Bjerknes et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature on cell type-specific functional properties.

claim: The delayed structural maturation of pyramidal cells might reflect the delayed functional maturation of grid cells.
source: Grid and border cells have been implicated to be largely specific to pyramidal and stellate cells respectively (Tang et al., 2014)and the delayed structural maturation of pyramidal cells might reflect the delayed functional maturation of grid cells (Wills et al., 2010; Langston et al., 2010), with the converse being applicable to stellate and border cells (Bjerknes et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on inference from correlation between structural and functional maturation timelines, supported by citations.

claim: The early structural maturation of stellate cells might reflect the early functional maturation of border cells.
source: Grid and border cells have been implicated to be largely specific to pyramidal and stellate cells respectively (Tang et al., 2014)and the delayed structural maturation of pyramidal cells might reflect the delayed functional maturation of grid cells (Wills et al., 2010; Langston et al., 2010), with the converse being applicable to stellate and border cells (Bjerknes et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on inference from the converse relationship mentioned for stellate cells and border cells.

claim: Pyramidal cells project to CA1 and contralateral MEC.
source: The divergent projection patterns of pyramidal and stellate cells, with the former projecting to CA1 (Kitamura et al., 2014) and contralateral MEC (Varga et al., 2010) and the latter to dentate gyrus (Varga et al., 2010; Ray et al., 2014) and deep layers of MEC (Sürmeli et al., 2015), have differing theoretical interpretations in spatial information processing.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on projection patterns.

claim: Stellate cells project to dentate gyrus and deep layers of MEC.
source: The divergent projection patterns of pyramidal and stellate cells, with the former projecting to CA1 (Kitamura et al., 2014) and contralateral MEC (Varga et al., 2010) and the latter to dentate gyrus (Varga et al., 2010; Ray et al., 2014) and deep layers of MEC (Sürmeli et al., 2015), have differing theoretical interpretations in spatial information processing.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on projection patterns.

claim: The divergent projection patterns of pyramidal and stellate cells have differing theoretical interpretations in spatial information processing.
source: The divergent projection patterns of pyramidal and stellate cells, with the former projecting to CA1 (Kitamura et al., 2014) and contralateral MEC (Varga et al., 2010) and the latter to dentate gyrus (Varga et al., 2010; Ray et al., 2014) and deep layers of MEC (Sürmeli et al., 2015), have differing theoretical interpretations in spatial information processing.
evidence: Represents established knowledge about functional implications of projection patterns.

claim: The same sets of neurons corresponding to grid and border cells have been implicated to be differentially involved in temporal association memory and contextual memory respectively.
source: The same sets of neurons, which correspond to grid and border cells (Tang et al., 2014), have also been implicated to be differentially involved in temporal association memory (Kitamura et al., 2014) and contextual memory (Kitamura et al., 2015) respectively.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on memory functions.

claim: An underlying differential structural maturation timeline of the microcircuit governing these processes may translate into a differential functional maturation profile of these memories.
source: An underlying differential structural maturation timeline of the microcircuit governing these processes may also translate into a differential functional maturation profile of these memories.
evidence: Based on speculation about relationship between structural and functional maturation.

claim: The structural maturation of medial entorhinal cortex can be coarsely divided into an early appearance of the calbindin+ neuron patches and a progressive cell-type specific refinement of the cellular structure, which proceeds along the dorsal to ventral axis.
source: We conclude that the structural maturation of medial entorhinal cortex can be coarsely divided into an early appearance of the calbindin+ neuron patches and a progressive cell-type specific refinement of the cellular structure, which proceeds along the dorsal to ventral axis.
evidence: Represents a summary conclusion based on all the developmental observations presented.

claim: Male and female Wistar rats from E18 to P24 and adults (>P42) were used in the study.
source: Male and female Wistar rats (n=83) from E18 to P24 and adults (>P42) were used in the study.
evidence: Describes the experimental subjects used.

claim: The ages of rats were accurate to ± 1 day.
source: The ages were accurate to ± 1 day.
evidence: Describes the precision of age determination.

claim: Wolframin is a marker which co-localizes with calbindin+ pyramidal neurons in layer 2 of MEC in adult rodents.
source: Third, wolframin expression, a marker which co-localizes with calbindin+ pyramidal neurons in layer 2 of MEC in adult rodents (Kitamura et al., 2014), develops from dorsal to ventral in layer 2 medial entorhinal cortex and parasubiculum (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Studies suggest the early emergence of head-directional selectivity in the cortico-hippocampal system.
source: The functional development of spatial response properties has also been investigated in the cortico-hippocampal system (Ainge and Langston, 2012; Wills et al., 2014), with studies suggesting the early emergence of head-directional selectivity (Tan et al., 2015; Bjerknes et al., 2015), border representation (Bjerknes et al., 2014) and place cell firing, but a delayed maturation of grid cell discharges (Wills et al., 2010; Langston et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Studies suggest the early emergence of border representation in the cortico-hippocampal system.
source: The functional development of spatial response properties has also been investigated in the cortico-hippocampal system (Ainge and Langston, 2012; Wills et al., 2014), with studies suggesting the early emergence of head-directional selectivity (Tan et al., 2015; Bjerknes et al., 2015), border representation (Bjerknes et al., 2014) and place cell firing, but a delayed maturation of grid cell discharges (Wills et al., 2010; Langston et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Studies suggest the early emergence of place cell firing in the cortico-hippocampal system.
source: The functional development of spatial response properties has also been investigated in the cortico-hippocampal system (Ainge and Langston, 2012; Wills et al., 2014), with studies suggesting the early emergence of head-directional selectivity (Tan et al., 2015; Bjerknes et al., 2015), border representation (Bjerknes et al., 2014) and place cell firing, but a delayed maturation of grid cell discharges (Wills et al., 2010; Langston et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Studies suggest a delayed maturation of grid cell discharges in the cortico-hippocampal system.
source: The functional development of spatial response properties has also been investigated in the cortico-hippocampal system (Ainge and Langston, 2012; Wills et al., 2014), with studies suggesting the early emergence of head-directional selectivity (Tan et al., 2015; Bjerknes et al., 2015), border representation (Bjerknes et al., 2014) and place cell firing, but a delayed maturation of grid cell discharges (Wills et al., 2010; Langston et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Remarkably little is known about the structural development of the microcircuits which bring about spatial properties in the hippocampal formation.
source: Even though there is information on the emergence of functional spatial properties in the hippocampal formation, remarkably little is known about the structural development of the microcircuits which bring about these properties.
evidence: Represents a knowledge gap that motivates the study.
